item.question: A toy 10 cm tall stands 50 cm in front of a wall. A torch shines straight at the wall from 50 cm in front of the toy. How tall is the shadow? What if the torch is moved to 150 cm in front of the toy?
steps: The rays spread from the torch, so the shadow and the toy make similar triangles.
Torch to wall is 50 + 50 = 100 cm, twice the torch to toy distance.
With the torch at 150 cm, torch to wall is 150 + 50 = 200 cm.
Shadow = 10 × 200 ÷ 150 ≈ 13.3 cm, closer to the toy's 10 cm.
item.answer: 20 cm, then about 13.3 cm: the farther the torch, the closer the shadow is to the projection

item.question: A square card has diagonals of 10 cm. It is tilted in sunlight about one diagonal, so the other diagonal's shadow is 6 cm. What is the shadow, and how long is each side?
steps: The diagonal on the hinge stays 10 cm; the other diagonal's shadow is 6 cm.
The shadows of the diagonals still cross at right angles at their midpoints, and opposite sides stay parallel.
So the shadow is a rhombus with diagonals 10 cm and 6 cm.
Each side = √(5² + 3²) = √34, about 5.83 cm.
item.answer: A rhombus with sides of about 5.83 cm

item.question: Imagine eight identical cubes, glued together along faces to form the letter C. (i) This looks like a C from the front. What does it look like from the side? From the top? (ii) Glue additional cubes to make a shape that looks like one letter from the front and another from the top. (iii) Now, can you glue even more cubes to make it look like three given letters from the front, top and side? (iv) Can you think of other letter combinations to make with a single combination of cubes in this manner?
steps: The C is 4 cubes tall: a row of 3 on top, 1 cube on the left in each of the two middle rows, and a row of 3 at the bottom, 3 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 8.
From the side every row hides behind its first cube: a column of 4 squares, like the letter I.
From the top the rows stack under each other: a row of 3 squares.
For (ii) to (iv), add cubes behind the front letter so the top view spells the second letter, then check the side view.
item.answer: (i) From the side a column of 4 squares, from the top a row of 3 squares; (ii) to (iv) are built by adding cubes behind the letter

item.question: A glass cube balanced on a corner is projected onto the floor. How many of its 12 edges form the hexagon outline, and how many lie inside it?
steps: The top and bottom corners both project to the centre of the hexagon.
The 3 edges at the top corner and the 3 at the bottom corner run from the centre outwards: 3 + 3 = 6 inside.
The remaining 12 − 6 = 6 edges form the outline.
All 12 projections have the same length, so the outline is a regular hexagon.
item.answer: 6 edges make the regular hexagon and 6 run inside from its centre

item.question: Observe this triangle. (i) Would it be possible to build a model out of actual cubes? What are the front, top, and side profiles of this impossible triangle? (ii) Recreate this on an isometric grid. (iii) Why does the illusion work?
steps: (i) No: each corner looks like a right angle bend, but three such bends cannot close into a triangle in real space. A real model of rows of cubes looks right only from one viewpoint.
(ii) Draw each arm as a row of cubes along a grid direction and join the ends where they appear to meet.
(iii) An isometric drawing loses depth: a near end and a far end can project to the same point, so the eye joins them.
item.answer: It cannot be built; the illusion works because the projection loses depth, so far and near ends appear to touch
